content:
When I ask an AI whether my plan is good, it usually says yes. A confident “looks good” that was never tested is the failure I worry about most. So I wrote two Claude Code skills that try to attack a plan instead of agreeing with it.
The first real use was on the skill itself. I asked the council to review its own design, and it unanimously argued for a change: stop saving sessions by default. I made that change.
One skill runs a council of isolated personas. The other asks a different model for a second opinion. I will explain both, and where they fall short.
What is the council? # /council starts several independent subagents. Each one attacks the question through a single lens, and then I combine their answers. The goal is disagreement, not consensus. A council that agrees with everything is worse than no council, because it gives false confidence.
graph TD Q[Question plus optional diff or files] --> P[Pick a panel] P --> A[Persona 1] P --> B[Persona 2] P --> C[Persona 3 to 5] A --> S[Chairman synthesis] B --> S C --> S S --> R[Verdict, confidence, preserved dissent] How is it built? # Seven design choices matter.
Isolation. Each persona runs in its own context and never sees the others, so they cannot anchor on each other’s answers. Panels by question type. There are product, code, architecture and debug panels. The architecture panel uses Contrarian-Risk, First-Principles, Operability-SRE, Cost-and-Complexity and Executor. A shared contract. Every persona must raise at least three concrete objections tied to the real artifact, such as a file and line or the exact claim. Generic praise is banned, and approving is not allowed. Structured output. Each persona returns a verdict, its objections, its single biggest risk and the one thing it would fix. That makes the synthesis mechanical. Dissent is kept. A minority view is recorded, not averaged away. If the lenses fundamentally disagree, confidence is LOW and the output says the decision is mine to make. An anti-ceremony guard. Trivial or factual questions skip the council. Optional rigor. --review adds an anonymized peer round and a judge that critiques the discussion itself. --quick uses three cheap personas. It also saves nothing by default. The council reviewed its own skill and argued for that. Saved sessions contain architecture and security reasoning, backup tools can sync them off the machine, and nothing ever expires them. So saving is opt-in with --save.
What is the limit? # Isolated contexts give independent reasoning, but every persona is still the same model with the same training biases. The judge is the same model too. Independence is not diversity. For a high-stakes call, I want a different model in the loop.
What are second opinions from other models? # That is the second family of skills: /ask-codex, /ask-cursor, /ask-opus and /ask-fable. Each one starts a read-only reviewer subagent. The subagent runs a different CLI against the repo and returns a structured verdict.
/ask-codex runs the OpenAI Codex CLI. /ask-cursor runs Cursor’s headless agent. /ask-opus and /ask-fable run claude -p with a larger model at high effort. They help when the main session is on a cheaper model. The verdict has a fixed shape (AGREE, DISAGREE or CONCERNS) with concrete citations, and the reviewer cannot edit anything. Each call has a budget cap, so a quick second look does not turn into a surprise bill.
How do I use them? # For a trivial question, I just ask. No ceremony. For a real fork in the road, I run /council with the matching panel. For a high-stakes or hard-to-reverse decision, I run the council with --review, then one cross-model reviewer on the result. What would I change? # I have not measured how often this changes an outcome, so I treat it as a habit, not a proof. What it does reliably is make me write down the strongest objection before I commit. That alone has been worth the extra minute.
What I would change next is a small log of decisions with the council’s verdict and what actually happened, so I can check whether it helps. I do not have that data yet.
Thanks for reading.
title: A Council of Disagreeing Agents, and Second Opinions From Other Models

content:
I use Claude Code every day. Right now my ~/.claude/projects folder holds 134 sessions and about 1 GB of transcripts. I usually remember what I worked on, but not which project it was in, and /resume does not help. So I built a small terminal tool called ClaudeLens to fix it.
This post covers what it does, how it finds sessions, and one resume bug that took me a while to understand.
What is the problem? # Two things make old sessions hard to find.
First, names you set with /rename are not indexed for search. This is a known issue. Second, the picker only looks at the current project, so a session from another project never shows up.
What does ClaudeLens do? # It lists the sessions from every project in one place. You search, read the conversation, and resume with one key.
Cross-project list. Every session from every project. Layered search. A fast index search, plus optional semantic search through claude-mem if you run it. Preview. Scroll the conversation before you commit to resuming it. One-key resume. In a new tab on iTerm2, Terminal.app and tmux, or in the current tab on Warp. Install and run it:
go install github.com/KaushalDokania/claudelens@latest claudelens --search "auth refactor" How does it find sessions? # It does not have a database or a background process. It reads what Claude Code already writes under ~/.claude/.
~/.claude/projects/*/sessions-index.json summaries, timestamps, branches ~/.claude/sessions/*.json names from /rename (active sessions) ~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl full conversation, used for preview localhost:37777 (optional) claude-mem: summaries and semantic search In simple words, it cannot get out of sync with Claude Code, because it only reads Claude Code’s own files.
Why does claude --resume say “no conversation found”? # This is the bug that cost me time. claude --resume <id> only works when you run it from the right directory. The right directory is the one whose encoded name matches the session’s storage folder under ~/.claude/projects/. The encoding replaces every character that is not a letter or digit with -. So /Users/me/work/my.repo is stored as -Users-me-work-my-repo.
The catch is that a session can move. I start in the main checkout, switch to a git worktree halfway, and the transcript now records more than one working directory. If I resume from the wrong one, Claude Code says it found nothing, even though the session is sitting on disk.
ClaudeLens reads every working directory recorded in the session. It picks the one that encodes to the real storage folder, not just the first one it saw.
How does it resume in a new tab? # It depends on the terminal.
Terminal What ClaudeLens does iTerm2 New tab through AppleScript Terminal.app New window through AppleScript tmux tmux new-window Warp Resumes in the current tab Warp was the awkward one. It has no AppleScript support, and its warp:// URL scheme cannot run commands. My first attempts relied on that URL scheme and were unreliable, and I dropped them. What works is replacing the ClaudeLens process itself with claude --resume in the right directory. That is one keypress and nothing to break. If it is not possible, ClaudeLens falls back to a Warp tab config, and then to copying the full cd && claude --resume ... command to the clipboard.
What did I learn about Bubbletea layouts? # Many of my early commits were layout fixes, which says something. Three things finally made the panes stable:
Clip everything to exact sizes. Pad or truncate each pane to its width and height, then hard-clip the whole View() to the terminal height. Truncate with ANSI awareness. Cutting a styled string by bytes breaks the escape codes. Use lipgloss Width and MaxWidth instead of len. Draw the borders yourself. Lipgloss borders fought with my height clipping. A small box-drawing function was simpler. What would I change? # I would add the recording first. A one-minute demo explains the tool better than this post does. I would also look at whether the worktree handling can be simplified, since it only exists because sessions move between directories.
ClaudeLens is MIT licensed and small. If you lose sessions the way I do, try it, and open an issue if it does not find yours: github.com/KaushalDokania/claudelens.
Thanks for reading.
title: Claude Code Can't Find Your Renamed Sessions, So I Built ClaudeLens

content:
I built a small tool called Sentinel that answers one question: what needs my attention right now? It collects data from my chat, issue tracker, code host, notes app and AI sessions, and writes one local HTML page. A Claude Code skill does the collecting. I have not measured how much time it saves.
What problem does it solve? # My work state lives in five places. Chat has mentions. The issue tracker has tickets. The code host has pull requests and failing checks. The notes app has tasks. My AI sessions have half-finished work.
Checking each one is slow. Worse, none of them tells me which item matters most. I wanted one list, sorted by urgency.
What is a “collector”? # A collector is a small unit that reads one source and returns JSON in a fixed shape. In simple words, it is an adapter with no side effects.
Sentinel has one collector per source. Each one runs in parallel. If one fails, the dashboard still renders the others and shows a warning in the failed panel.
How does it work end to end? # config.json -> collectors (parallel) -> action items -> HTML + JSON Read a config file. Each source has an enabled flag. Run all enabled collectors at once. Merge the results into a single priority list. Embed the data as JSON in a self-contained HTML file. Open the file in the browser. The page uses inline CSS and vanilla JavaScript. It has no build step and works from a file:// path. The raw JSON is also saved next to it, which makes debugging easy.
How does it decide what is urgent? # The rules are simple and written down. They are not a model’s guess. These are the kinds of rules I use:
A critical-priority ticket is critical. A pull request with a failing check is high. A review request waiting on me is medium. A chat mention that contains a question or an action word is medium. A task past its due date is high. A thread I joined that has new replies is low. The list is sorted by urgency, then by recency. I feel plain rules are the right call here. I can read them, argue with them and change them in a minute.
Why a Claude Code skill and not a script? # Some sources I reach through command line tools. Others I reach through MCP connectors that already hold my login. A skill lets Claude call both and write the glue.
The skill is a markdown file that describes the steps, the JSON shapes and the safety rules. The same file runs by hand, from a shell wrapper using claude -p, or on a recurring schedule.
The cost is that every refresh runs a model session. A plain script would be faster and cheaper per run. I did not compare the two.
Which options did I reject? # A hosted dashboard: it would need my data on someone else’s server. Write access to the sources: a dashboard that posts or edits is a risk I do not need. Sentinel is read-only. A framework front end: I considered one for the layout. A single static file was easier to keep working. Historical charts: I left them out of scope. The page shows now, not trends. What went wrong? # One source exposes calendar events in a format my connector could not parse. I disabled that collector instead of working around it. A search for “my pull requests” returned nothing until I used the author filter instead of the assignee filter. Assignee is rarely set. Scheduled sessions expire after a while, so auto-refresh needs renewing. I have not found a clean fix. What would I change? # I would move the collection step out of the model and into a plain script, and keep the model only for summarising. It would be cheaper and more repeatable. I would also store each refresh, so I could see how my queue changes over a week.
I would also keep secrets and identifiers out of the skill file from day one, and load them from a config file instead.
Thanks for reading.
title: Sentinel: A Personal Command Center Dashboard

content:
What are Go Packages? # Modularity and code reusability are among the essential pillars of good software engineering practices. Functions are the first layer of code reusability in any programming language. Go takes it to another level by providing a different mechanism: packages.
According to the official Go documentation: How to write Go code
Go programs are organized into packages. A package is a collection of source files in the same directory that are compiled together. Functions, types, variables, and constants defined in one source file are visible to all other source files within the same package.
In simple words, a package is a directory within a Go workspace containing one or more Go source files, which may also include other packages.
Syntax # Every Go source file must belong to some package. The first line of the file should declare the package name like this.
package <package_name> All the functions, types and variables present in this source file, now belong to the declared package and can be imported in other packages using the package name(as long as they are exported).
Example # Almost all Go programs contain this line.
import "fmt" fmt is one the core packages provided by Go installation which contains several functionalities related to input/output formatting. Once imported, we can use functions exported by this package like fmt.Print(), fmt.Printf(), fmt.Scanf().
Exported and Un-exported names # The members of a package imported in another package can only be accessed when the are ’exported’. A function, type or variable is said to be exported only when it’s name starts with a capital letter.
So, exported members(function, type or variable) starts with capital letters and can be accessed outside of package.
While everything else which does not start with a capital letter is said to be un-exported and is visible only within the package it was declared.
main package # Like other programming languages, Go also has main() function as the entry point of the program. The main() function can only be present within a special package main. When main package is compiled it generates an executable file as output.
In Go, a package can server either of the two purposes.
Commands: The programs with main package, i.e. with executables are called Commands Packages: While the others non-main packages are simply called Packages for code-reusability. Example # Let’s write a simple ‘Hello World’ program to
package main import ( "fmt" ) func main() { fmt.Print("Hello World!") } When we run this program with the go run we can see the output in the console.
Output
$ go run hello.go Hello World!$ We can run go build to simply generate the executable file which then can be run directly or shared with others to run on other machine as independent executable file.
Output
$ go build -o hello $ ls hello* hello.go $ ./hello Hello World!$ Here, the option -o is used to specify the name of the output file being generated
Note: Use hello.exe as the output file name for Windows systems.
Importing packages # There are two possible format/syntax to import packages in Go.
// Multiple import statements import "fmt" import "time" import "math/rand" // Factored import statements import ( "fmt" "time" "math/rand" ) In Go the package name is the same as the last element of the import path. Say for example, rand is the actual package name to be used while importing the package "math/rand"
Naming imports # In Go the imports can be named as well. See below
import ( "fmt" "time" r "math/rand" ) Here, r is the named import which can be used in place of rand to access its member functions or types.
Why packages? # The way Go bundles the packages has following benefits
Lesser naming conflicts: Multiple packages may have functions with same names Code organization: Modularity pays off in the way that code organization becomes efficient and finding the code that we want to reuse becomes easier Faster compilation: Go compiler works smartly and compiles only those packages which have been modified. So, the fmt package which is included in most of the programs doesn’t need to be compiled while compiling our program. Conclusion # While Go is still a fairly new langague, there are several useful standard library packages. Go’s package management provides lot of flexibility and helps fasten the development by better code organization.
title: Getting Started With Go Packages

content:
We spend a lot of time on Linux bash shell either using Git, writing/running scripts, building/serving applications or analyzing server logs. That’s why we need a bash prompt which gives us important information and is also easy to read. To improve the look and feel even further you can also add colors to your PS1 prompt.
What is PS1? # PS1(Prompt String 1) is one of the shell prompts available in Linux/Unix. Once you log into a machine, you are presented with a prompt like kaushal@ubuntu:~ $ where you enter commands to run. Here, $ represents a normal user while the root user is represented by #. On most Linux distros the PS1 prompt displays the current user, hostname and current directory by default.
What are the different PS variables? # According to the bash documentation:
PS1 The value of this parameter is expanded (see PROMPTING below) and used as the primary prompt string. The default value is ``\s-\v\$ ''. PS2 The value of this parameter is expanded as with PS1 and used as the secondary prompt string. The default is ``> ''. PS3 The value of this parameter is used as the prompt for the select command (see SHELL GRAMMAR above). PS4 The value of this parameter is expanded as with PS1 and the value is printed before each command bash displays during an execution trace. The first character of PS4 is replicated mul‐ tiple times, as necessary, to indicate multiple levels of indi‐ rection. The default is ``+ ''. So, PS1 is the the first prompt string which you see and where you enter commands to run, PS2 is the continuation prompt which comes up in case the command you entered is incomplete or the primary command needs more inputs, PS3 is shown when select command waits for input, and PS4 shows the debugging trace line prefix during the execution of any command or script.
How to know your current PS1 variable? # Simply print the PS1 value using echo
echo $PS1 Output prompt: [\u@\h \W]$
The following is the list of escape characters supported by the PS variables in Linux.
\a - A bell character. \d - The date, in "Weekday Month Date" format (e.g., "Tue May 26"). \D{format} - The format is passed to strftime(3) and the result is inserted into the prompt string; an empty format results in a locale-specific time representation. The braces are required. \e - An escape character. \h - The hostname, up to the first ‘.’. \H - The hostname. \j - The number of jobs currently managed by the shell. \l - The basename of the shell’s terminal device name. \n - A newline. \r - A carriage return. \s - The name of the shell, the basename of $0 (the portion following the final slash). \t - The time, in 24-hour HH:MM:SS format. \T - The time, in 12-hour HH:MM:SS format. \@ - The time, in 12-hour am/pm format. \A - The time, in 24-hour HH:MM format. \u - The username of the current user. \v - The version of Bash (e.g., 2.00) \V - The release of Bash, version + patchlevel (e.g., 2.00.0) \w - The current working directory, with $HOME abbreviated with a tilde (uses the $PROMPT_DIRTRIM variable). \W - The basename of $PWD, with $HOME abbreviated with a tilde \! - The history number of this command. \# - The command number of this command. \$ - If the effective uid is 0, #, otherwise $. \nnn - The character whose ASCII code is the octal value nnn. \\ - A backslash. \[ - Begin a sequence of non-printing characters. This could be used to embed a terminal control sequence into the prompt. \] - End a sequence of non-printing characters. How to modify or change the PS1 prompt? # To modify the prompt simply set the PS1 environment variable with the desired value.
PS1="Welcome user" Output prompt: Welcome user
More Examples # To set PS1 to your current directory you can use
PS1="$PWD> " Output prompt: /home/kaushal>
Note: This prompt is static and will not change when you move to a new directory.
Now, let us change the prompt to display today’s date and hostname:
PS1="\d \h $ " Output prompt: Sun Feb 23 ubuntu $
Below PS1 will display date/time, hostname and the current working directory.
PS1="[\d \t \u@\h:\w ] $ " Output prompt: [Sun Feb 23 18:01:40 kaushal@ubuntu:~ ] $
You can also use functions in PS1 prompt. Suppose you want to track free RAM available then add the below function in your ~/.bashrc file
free_ram () { free -m | awk ‘{print $4}’ | head -2 | tail -1; }
and set the PS1 value to
PS1='$(free_ram)Mb [\u@\h \W]$ ' Output prompt: **1764Mb [kaushal@ubuntu ~]$
You can also divide the prompt into multiple lines using \n for long commands
PS1="[\t]\w\n\u@\h:$" Output prompt:
[18:32:13]~/workspace
kaushal@ubuntu:$
Making the changes permanent # When you set the PS1 in the console the changes are temporarily and are available only for that session. To make the changes permanent add the PS1 variable in your user profile file.
nano ~/.bashrc To save, hit CTRL + X and enter Y. The changes will come in affect next time you login to the terminal.
Modifying ~/.bashrc causes changes to be applicable only for the current user. To make the changes permanent for all the users add the PS1 variable to the following file
/etc/bashrc for Redhat and friends /etc/bash.bashrc for Debian/Ubuntu /etc/bash.bashrc.local for Suse and others Conclusion # Modifying the bash prompt is pretty easy and very helpful as it can display any extra information we need. We can also add styles to the PS1 prompt using colors which makes the prompt pleasing to the eyes and more readable in case your screen is full of several commands and outputs.
Thanks for reading.
title: How to Customize Linux PS1 Bash Prompt
